title: Frequency Response of Differential Pairs
intro: A fully differential pair behaves like its CS half circuit for differential signals. Two effects are new: the common-mode rejection degrades at high frequency because of the tail-node capacitance, and a current-mirror load adds a 'mirror pole' and a left-half-plane zero.

blocks.text: Passive loads: differential and common mode

For differential inputs the half circuit is a CS stage, with Miller multiplication of $C_{GD}$ and the same poles. Both halves share one transfer function, so the differential output has as many poles as one half, not twice as many.

For common-mode inputs the tail node P matters. Its capacitance $C_P$ (from $C_{GD3}$, $C_{DB3}$, $C_{SB1}$, $C_{SB2}$) can be large because the tail device is made wide to save headroom. Replacing $r_{o3}$ by $r_{o3} \parallel (1/C_P s)$ and $R_D$ by $R_D \parallel (1/C_L s)$ in the low-frequency result with a $g_m$ mismatch $\Delta g_m$:

blocks.tex: \mathrm{CMRR} \approx \frac{g_m}{\Delta g_m}\left[1 + 2g_m\left(r_{o3} \parallel \frac{1}{C_P s}\right)\right] = \frac{g_m}{\Delta g_m}\cdot\frac{r_{o3}C_P s + 1 + 2g_m r_{o3}}{r_{o3}C_P s + 1}

blocks.text: with $g_m$ the average transconductance of the pair. The CMRR starts falling at the pole $1/(r_{o3}C_P)$ and levels at $g_m/\Delta g_m$ above the zero $(1 + 2g_m r_{o3})/(r_{o3}C_P) \approx 2g_m/C_P$.

blocks.alt: CMRR in dB against frequency on a log axis: flat at about 72 dB up to roughly 40 MHz, then falling at 20 dB per decade, then flattening at about 34 dB above roughly 3 GHz.
blocks.caption: CMRR against frequency for the values of problem 2.

blocks.text: Practical consequence: high-frequency noise on the supply or ground moves node P through $C_P$, and with mismatch it turns into differential output noise, increasingly so above $1/(2\pi r_{o3}C_P)$. Low supply voltages make it worse: a wider tail device saves headroom but adds $C_P$.

With PMOS current-source loads (fully differential), differential swings at the two drains inject opposite currents through $C_{GD3}$ and $C_{GD4}$ into the shared load-gate node, so it stays an AC ground. The half circuit is the CS stage with $R_D$ replaced by $r_{o1} \parallel r_{o3}$; that large resistance makes the output pole $1/[(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o3})C_L]$ dominant, which is the starting point of op-amp compensation.
Active current-mirror load: the mirror pole

blocks.alt: Five-transistor OTA: NMOS input pair M1 and M2 with tail current ISS; PMOS mirror M3 (diode-connected, node E) and M4. Capacitor CE from node E to ground; the output at the drain of M4 has load capacitor CL.
blocks.caption: Two signal paths with different transfer functions: a slow one through the mirror node E and a fast one straight to the output.

blocks.text: Half of the signal reaches the output through M3 and M4, passing node E, whose resistance is about $1/g_{m3}$ and whose capacitance $C_E$ includes $C_{GS3}$, $C_{GS4}$, $C_{DB3}$, $C_{DB1}$ and Miller contributions. This gives a mirror pole near $g_{m3}/C_E$; PMOS devices have poor $g_m$ per unit $C_{GS}$, so this pole often matters. With a Thevenin model of the input pair ($V_X = g_{mN}r_{oN}V_{in}$, $R_X = 2r_{oN}$):

blocks.tex: \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{g_{mN}r_{oN}(2g_{mP} + C_E s)r_{oP}}{2r_{oP}r_{oN}C_E C_L s^2 + \left[(2r_{oN} + r_{oP})C_E + r_{oP}(1 + 2g_{mP}r_{oN})C_L\right]s + 2g_{mP}(r_{oN} + r_{oP})}

blocks.text: With the mirror pole far above the output pole:

The left-half-plane zero at twice the mirror pole follows from adding the two paths: $\frac{A_0}{1 + s/\omega_{p1}}\left(\frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_{p2}} + 1\right)$ has a numerator $2 + s/\omega_{p2}$. A fully differential pair with current-source loads has no mirror pole, one more reason to prefer it.

Not every fully differential circuit escapes: if the signal current is folded through current mirrors (say $1:K$ mirrors into resistive loads, gain $g_{m1}KR_D$), each mirror's diode node adds a pole near $g_{m3}/C_X$, with $C_X$ including $C_{GS3}$, $C_{GS5}$ and the Miller-multiplied $C_{GD5}$.

blocks.title: Mirror pole and zero
blocks.text: A five-transistor OTA has $g_{m3} = g_{mP} = 1\text{ mS}$, $C_E = 400\text{ fF}$, $r_{oN} = r_{oP} = 40\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C_L = 500\text{ fF}$. Find the output pole, the mirror pole and the zero.
solution: Output: $r_{oN} \parallel r_{oP} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, $f_{p1} = 1/(2\pi \cdot 20\text{ k}\Omega \cdot 500\text{ fF}) = 15.9\text{ MHz}$.
blocks.answer: 15.9 MHz, 398 MHz, and an LHP zero at 796 MHz.

blocks.title: CMRR roll-off
blocks.text: A resistively loaded pair has $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$ per device, a 2% transconductance mismatch, a tail device with $r_{o3} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$ and $C_P = 200\text{ fF}$. Find the low-frequency CMRR, the frequency where it starts to fall, and its high-frequency floor.
solution: $g_m/\Delta g_m = 50$; $1 + 2g_m r_{o3} = 81$; low-frequency CMRR $= 4050$, or 72.1 dB.
Zero: $\approx 2g_m/(2\pi C_P) = 3.18\text{ GHz}$; above it CMRR $\to g_m/\Delta g_m = 50$ (34 dB).
blocks.answer: 72 dB, falling from about 40 MHz to a 34 dB floor above about 3 GHz.
